summary: Defines a set of managed objects, in the SNMP Management Information Base, for monitoring Ethernet-like network interfaces. It lets management software read statistics and status for these links in a standard way. It was replaced by RFC 1398.

eli5.summary: A scoreboard for a network cable. This document lists the numbers a network helper can read to see how well an Ethernet connection is doing, so every brand of equipment reports it the same way.

questions: how to monitor ethernet interface with snmp
subtitle: SNMP management objects for Ethernet and Ethernet-like interface monitoring

tldr.problem: Ethernet networks needed standardized SNMP objects to monitor interface status, performance, and errors across different vendors' equipment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three groups of managed objects based on IEEE 802.3 specifications: generic Ethernet interface controls, statistics for normal operation, and collision statistics. All objects follow the standard MIB framework.
tldr.outcome: This provides comprehensive visibility into Ethernet link health and performance. It was later updated by RFC 1398 to add additional management capabilities.

today: RFC 1284 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1398, which provides updated definitions with additional management capabilities for Ethernet and higher-speed network interfaces.

sections.title: Standard Interface Monitoring
sections.content:
RFC 1284 defines the Management Information Base (MIB) for Ethernet-like interfaces, providing SNMP-based monitoring for Ethernet, IEEE 802.3, and similar networks. The RFC is based on the IEEE 802.3 Layer Management Specification and provides objects for three types of Ethernet-like media: ethernet-csmacd, iso88023-csmacd, and starLan.

All Ethernet-like interfaces are identified using a common object identifier in the MIB tree called dot3. The definitions avoid duplicating objects already present in MIB-II for generic interface statistics (such as octet and frame counts), and instead focus on Ethernet-specific measurements and controls defined by the IEEE 802.3 standard.
sections.eli5: Ethernet is the most common type of network cable. This document says what numbers a network manager can read to see how well Ethernet connections are working.

sections.title: Generic Ethernet Control Group
sections.content:
The generic Ethernet-like group provides control and status information for each interface. The MAC address and initialization status can be managed, allowing operators to control whether the MAC and Physical Layer Signaling subsystems are initialized. The MAC sublayer status can be enabled or disabled, which affects both transmission and reception of frames.

Multicast frame reception can be independently controlled for each interface. The transmit enabled object controls whether MAC frame transmission is active. A diagnostic Time Domain Reflectometry (TDR) test value is available from the most recently executed TDR test, providing information about cable length and continuity.
sections.eli5: This group gives you controls and status for each Ethernet connection. You can turn sending and receiving on or off, and see if a cable test was done.

sections.title: Frame Statistics and Error Counters
sections.content:
The Ethernet-like statistics group provides extensive counters for frame transmission and reception errors. Alignment errors count frames that are not an integral number of octets long and fail the Frame Check Sequence (FCS) test. FCS error counters track frames of correct length that fail the checksum.

Collision statistics distinguish between single-collision frames (transmitted despite exactly one collision) and multiple-collision frames. Late collision counts detect collisions that occur more than 512 bit-times (51.2 microseconds) into transmission, indicating potential cable length problems. Excessive collision counters track frames that fail after too many collision attempts.
sections.eli5: These counters are like a health checkup: they count alignment errors, checksum failures, and collisions on the network. Too many errors might mean there is a problem with the cable or connection.

sections.title: Physical Layer and Transmission Errors
sections.content:
Carrier sense errors indicate times when the Medium Access Control sublayer could not sense the carrier signal when attempting to transmit, suggesting physical layer problems. SQE Test Error counters track signal quality errors reported by the Physical Layer Signaling sublayer.

Deferred transmission counters track frames whose first transmission attempt was delayed because the medium was busy. Excessive deferral counters track frames that waited too long for the medium to become free. Internal MAC transmit and receive errors capture hardware-level errors not covered by other counters. Frame too long errors track oversized received frames, while in-range and out-of-range length errors catch frames with incorrect length fields.
sections.eli5: These counters track physical problems like a lost carrier signal, frames that had to wait to be sent, and frames that are the wrong size.

sections.title: IEEE 802.3 Standards and SNMP Integration
sections.content:
The definitions in this RFC are based directly on the IEEE 802.3 Layer Management Specification, which includes Pascal pseudocode describing when and how various MAC attributes are measured and how MAC actions affect these measurements. Implementors should note that IEEE 802.3 explicitly describes the effects of MAC actions invoked through the MIB objects.

Due to implementation restrictions in some network hardware chipsets, some counters may be difficult or impossible to implement accurately. Vendors are encouraged to document in user guides when counter values may underestimate true occurrences. In the extreme case of total inability to detect certain errors, those counters will always be zero, but operators can still rely on counters that are implemented.
sections.eli5: This MIB is based on the official Ethernet standard, so every network equipment maker can implement it the same way. Sometimes hardware makes some counts hard to track, but vendors should explain that in their manuals.
